blocks.x: Testing, testing. I'll be glad when you're dead. That's right. Those were lost, I'm afraid. They were just given to Kate Howard. They went. Bill Russell never intended to do anything with them. Yes, but there aren't very many old man Moses. That's right. There aren't many of those. I'll show you the ones where we were talking about yesterday, the Bakersfield thing. Yeah. We don't have the exact date. I don't either. You don't have the exact date? I'll make it September 1954. That's the closest I can come to it. But you see, I did put that. It's walking with the king, not the king, not T-H-E-E. Did they put T? Yeah. They put T-H-E-E. Oh, that's a terrible. That's a misprint, yeah. Yes, it should be walking with the king. And the same date, Lord Lord, yeah. That's right. That's Caledonia. Well, you see, now, we have same day evening, and... Well, that's a mistake. That's a mistake. That's a mistake. Both. Yeah. Well, both the same... Just one performance. Yeah. Well, that's... Get that started. And as we noted there... Afternoon are really concert performances, so they do not have any audience noises. They're not from a rehearsal that I know of. They did no rehearsing in that hall. Can you remember the name of the hall? Yes. Harvey Auditorium. Harvey. Harvey Auditorium. Vegas. Oh, what that is. But there was no rehearsal. So I don't know where they got... How they took it without any audience noise. There was no warm-up. Nothing like that. The band never did. They just... It's funny, because there are three or four tracks that which do sound very different. You know, that sound... Well, they might be... I think those are tracks... That Alfred Lyon had, and he used to fill out that record. That could be it. I think that's it. I'm not certain. But there's something in the back of my mind... That says... That he filled that record out with... Either with tracks that he had from a previous recording... Something like that. Or something like that. That's why they said that's it. Yeah. I'm almost certain of... Well, now, this is... We're interviewing Dr. Dorothy Tate, and this is December 21st, 1968. And first of all, let me just ask you, Dorothy, about what you told me yesterday, about how you first became manager of the band, and how business in Vegas feel with you. Well, I always connected my mind with the earthquakes. We had a summer of very severe earthquakes, and we would have them about every hour, and we were all terrified and couldn't sleep, and I used to lie awake listening to George Lewis records, not realizing at the time that the band was still active. And one day I got a postcard from a friend who said that they had spent the last four nights listening to the George Lewis band at the Beverly Cavern in Los Angeles, right on the... in Hollywood, really. And, well, it was a matter of hours. I was on my way down there to hear them. And that was when I first met George, and came back on Cloud 15. Of course, magnificent music. The band was at their peak. And, um, got in touch with the, um, a non-profit group in Bakersfield, the Seven Arts Cultural Organization, devoted to bringing, uh, various, uh, interesting cultural events to the town. And they agreed to sponsor the concert. Well, uh, they couldn't do it for a month, several months. Of course, the band had to go home. Well, one concert wouldn't pay the band's round-trip transportation, plus, uh, a fee for the concert. There had to be other engagements. Well, at that time, Nicholas Gangliano in New Orleans was managing the band. He's now a New Orleans attorney. And, uh, uh, we were pretty desperate. We didn't know just what we would, how we could manage it. So it was up to me to go out and find some other places for the band to play. And I had never done anything like that before in my life. But I managed to, to arrange about, oh, three or four additional dates, one of them at the Royal Room in Hollywood. Uh, which brought in enough to make it worthwhile for the band to come out and to pay their transportation on the trip. So, in other words, the, uh, concert which you had arranged in, in Bakersfield was, the, the band had already gone back to New Orleans by that time, when you arranged for them to come out and play there. No, uh, we made the arrangement while George was there. And I don't recall what, something happened. They were, uh, scheduled to be on the coast later. I don't remember exactly what it was. But something went, uh, wrong, as it frequently does with band arrangements. And it meant they only had that one engagement. And... This was the Bakersfield. This was the Bakersfield. And, and, and, and, and, and is, is this incidentally the engagement where this, uh, recording was made? That was where the recording was made without authorization. And I tracked it down to the people who made it and insisted that they give me the tapes. And I got in touch with Alfred Lyon, Blue Note Records. And we cleared it through the union. And they bought the tape, of course, paid them in. Uh, and, uh, so everything was ship-shaped. But I had to put up a bit of a fight to get the tape. Because, of course, one thing that makes me furious is, is a bootleg tape. To me, this is the unforgivable. Oh. But, uh, anyway, we... But did, at this point on, then, after they came out, then, September 54, uh, presumably Nick Gagliano kind of withdrew from the managership of the band, and you were... Well, Nick went, uh, was starting in law school about then. He had them booked on a, um, college concert tour, uh, and was himself not able to go, and asked me if I would go with the band on the tour. And, uh, which I did. I was tickled to death, of course. And I don't know, it sort of worked out gradually. Yes. And then I, I was able to get them some, uh, club dates in San Francisco and on the coast. And then, uh, it was sort of a gradual thing. And you had had really no previous experience in this business of booking? None whatsoever. And I've never booked any. How did you go about doing this? I mean, is this something you felt that you had, well, I'd have a flair for? Well, you... Well, I'd have a flair for, do you think? No, I didn't feel it. I had a flair for it. It scared me to death. I, uh, uh, we booked them at the, uh, uh, China Lake military, uh, establishment. I was going to ask you to start a little inspection China Lake. Yes, that was a beautiful... Right in the middle of the desert. Nothing around. And it was outdoors at night on a beautiful, warm, um, desert night. Clear moonlight. It was one of the, it was one of the loveliest concerts I think I've ever been to. And, uh, I was able to do that through people I knew. And, um, I, I've forgotten how I, uh, managed the, uh, somebody suggested that I try the Royal Room and I think we made it there. I think I made it booking there for them for two or three weeks. Hmm. But I can't recall, uh, just how I, how I, but somebody told me to see the man who was the, uh, who owned the Royal Room and I did and he was tickled to death to have them. And once he got them he was crazy about them, of course. Yes. And, uh, but I have never done anything like that before and believe me, we'll never do it again, but. Now, uh, were you managing the band at the time, now, at the time around about there, I think in early 55 was when Lawrence had a heart attack, I think. Yes, I was with Lawrence when he had this attack. It, uh, um, in fact I took him to the hospital that night. Where was he when he, when he. Playing at the, uh, Beverly Cavern. And, uh, was it. On the stand. And had an attack right on the stand. Right on the stand. It was what they call cerebral anoxia. And, uh, I think that's the proper name. And it was a terrifying thing. And I got him to the, uh, Hollywood Emergency Hospital and from there he was transferred to the Los Angeles General Hospital because it was much, uh, much too ill, of course, to be released from the hospital. And then he, uh, uh, returned, uh, returned home. Uh, he at that time had a very high blood pressure. And I was told by the doctors then, look, man shouldn't travel. I think Lawrence was always deeply hurt that, uh, he didn't go on future trips, but it was too great a risk. That did represent then more or less the end of his traveling. I think in fact he did travel again a little bit in 55 because I think, um, I believe he went to Boston or something. Didn't he go in for a while? Oh, wait a moment. He, uh, that was all part of the same thing. Uh, George Gano came up and took his place. Then Lawrence did come back during this same engagement, the latter part of this engagement. Uh, this was, and of course that was the same engagement on which, uh, later on in New York that, uh, whoops, George was taken sick. No, I don't mean, I'm not, I don't mean the same engagement, I mean the same period of time. No. But anyhow, later on, Lawrence did come up to, uh, Boston and play, uh. That was the time I believed in Tony Perentia was playing. Yes, Tony Perentia. Something like that. Uh, wait a minute. Lawrence didn't come up to Boston. Lawrence didn't come up to Boston. Lawrence didn't come up to Boston. Lawrence didn't come up to Boston. The band left Tony Perentia in Boston when they went back to New Orleans. Lawrence. No. I don't think he came back on the road with the band again at all. I don't think Lawrence came back again on the road with the band. I think that is, is a mistake. He was supposed to. But I do know that, and believe me, this is off the record. Tony Perentia stayed from Boston because he lost so much money at the horse races there. But he pulled out of it, of course. Let me ask you this. How did, uh, George Lewis like the, being in California? How did he like the California climate, California people? Oh, he loved it. Did he ever, did he ever talk about, um, leaving New Orleans or maybe, you know, how did he let him come up? Once in a while, once in a while, he would say that if he, uh, but if he, you know, left, uh, he would like to live in California, but George's, uh, mother was here, and his, uh, daughter, and, of course, Jeanette, was still alive at that time, and I doubt very much that George would ever have really left New Orleans. Yes. Because his, uh, his family roots were deep here. And while I don't think George thought of Stoker thinks it's the greatest place in the world, at the same time, I think his, his, his deep attachment to his family, uh, he would never have really left here. It would have been just a, an idea, you know, well, it might be nice to live in California. Yes. He's, um, in fact, he has, he said to me one time, he said, my, um, my daddy's buried there, my mother's buried there, and my wife's buried there, and I'm gonna be buried there. And, um, so I think that, uh, nobody loved California. Yes, indeed, another place that he's very fond of, because he has so many good friends there, is Cincinnati. Because of the big following he has there, too, I think some of George's most enjoyable engagements were in Cincinnati. Did you, did you meet, um, Reverend Kirschwald? Oh my, yes, yes, indeed. Because I know he, he was, I think he probably helped. Yes, I went to, um, Oxford, uh, for a concert that the, uh, in fact we, that first trip we did a concert there. We had 50, uh, 54, 55 trip we, uh, played there. I remember it well. Lawrence Merrero had a birthday. We had Johnny Lucas with us on that trip, the trumpeter. Oh, yes. Tell me something about Bonadio. Oh, he's wonderful. He's a great person. You know he's in a wheelchair. Mm-hmm. And how badly handicapped he is. Oh, blowing a beautiful, um, cornet trumpet. And, um, lately he tells me that he's been doing the, um, not the slide trombone, the, um, Bell. Bell trombone. But, uh, he played a lovely trumpet. And George, George took care of him as though he'd been his own son. He helped him and they, uh, it was a very, a very lovely relationship. How much did he play with the band? Just that trip. And then, and he would play with them in, in Los Angeles. He would sit in with them often. But on that trip he, uh, uh, played, uh, oh, a number of engagements. He played in Chicago and, um, Oxford. He didn't play in Cincinnati. He didn't play in Cincinnati. But he played a number of concerts on that trip. Yeah. And he played at, uh, Purdue University, a concert there. Mm-hm. And, uh, it was a very happy trip. Mm-hm. Let me ask you about general sort of travel arrangements. Um, I don't like. Oh, no.
Oh, no.
Oh, no. I mean, how, uh, who shared rooms together? Oh, I, I don't know. I always tried to see to it that George had a room to himself.
Oh.

Because he was not in good health. He was in very frail health. And he had to sleep in the daytime and, uh, uh, get all the sleep. And I always tried to see if we couldn't work it that way. Drag and, uh, well, Drag and Joe Watkins always shared the room. Mm-hm. And let me see, uh, Elton Bernal. Well, then it just, but it was pretty standard, the Drag and, that Drag and Joe. Mm-hm. And George, whenever we possibly could, I'm trying to get him a room to himself. And then, I guess, the others, as I recall, it was... Jim Robinson or Kit Howard. Oh, yes. Jim Robinson and Kit Howard. That's true. Mm-hm. And then, I think, Elton and Lawrence quite often. Oh. Quite often. Did they have any special things that they would do on tour? I mean, did any, like, you know, particular job or something that had to be done would be done particularly by one person? No. Did they have anything like that? Well, no. They all, they had enough to do taking care of their instruments. Mm-hm. You know, Joe keeping track of his drums. Because I, I would keep track of them insofar as, uh, checking them, you know, and transportation and all that. But they, they, there was, there was plenty to do with, just as I say, keeping track of their instruments. And, no, no, nobody had any particular, uh, job. Did they, did they travel mainly by train or, or how would they live? Well, in those days, well, train or plane. Train or plane. They were, they were, I wouldn't have thought maybe at that time they would have been flying so much more. Oh yes, we, we flew a good deal. Yes, we, uh. Did they, did any of them have any particular aversion to that? Yes. Yes, Jim Robinson was terrified. Was one? It was, I think I have one here. It was his, his first plane trip and I don't remember what two cities, I don't remember what flight it was, but I do remember for some reason that it was on TWA. And, uh, he really was. He was, he was terribly apprehensive. And I had with me some very mild sedative pills. I don't know, I don't think they would really have affected a kitten. And, uh, but I gave it to him. And apparently it was the psychological effect. Because the pill itself could have had no effect. Mm-hm. And, uh, Jim kind of let out a sigh of relief, put his head back and fell asleep. And I'm sure it wasn't the, uh, pill I gave him. Um, what, uh, what do you, what is your impression on, or general feeling about the extent of George's popularity in America? Well, I think he has a hard core of fanatic fans. Uh, you only have to see them lined up outside those clubs in, in San Francisco and Chicago. In fact, anywhere. In fact, anywhere. You had only to see the crowds in New York. Pack them in. However. Where was this in New York? At the Paramount. Yes, that's the, uh, and that was, that's a huge place. Um, of course it's no longer there. Where was that? It was, uh, under the old Paramount Theater on Broadway. By Times Square, is that? Right by the Times building. The Times newspaper. And, uh, that place every weekend, not during the week, but weekends, that place was packed to the walls. How many people did it have? Six hundred and something. Good heavens. Yeah, it was a very large place. And, of course, at the Beverly Cavern in the Royal Room, they'd line up outside. Hmm. And, to get tables. And, uh, the same way, they got big crowds in Chicago. Everywhere he went. He drew them. But that does not necessarily mean that the younger people who don't know this music, uh, uh, I would say that George's popularity in this country is, is, uh, unequaled for, uh, or this rock bottom true jazz. That there isn't anybody who can, uh, better him. And I realize there's a man named Louis Armstrong. But, uh, uh, uh, he is no longer... No. ...represents that particular, what George represents. Right. Because George's music has never changed. And, um, uh, uh, oh, yes, I'd say he's popular among those who are New Orleans jazz, what they call buffs. Do you know if Louis Armstrong ever heard George Lewis play? Oh, mercy, yes. In this period? I mean, no. Of course, when he was back in the old days in New Orleans, he may have, well, even then he probably may have known. No, he didn't. You see, Louis left New Orleans when he was about 17 years old. Right. George never left until he was 45. Right. But, uh, uh, I'm sure Louis has heard him in, uh, well, in fact, I think Louis went to some of his concerts in London. Oh, is that right? Mm-hmm. Louis and he were in London at, uh, I think one engagement was, Louis was playing one concert, and I don't recall, but I'm, I'm, I'm very sure that he heard him in London. I know we heard Louis, and George always went backstage, and, uh, Louis is very fond of George. He sees things in the world. And, uh, Louis had a, I remember a young man, a fan of George's from Cincinnati, and, uh, he was, uh, at an Armstrong concert, and he wanted to, uh, he wanted to see Louis, he wanted to meet him. And, uh, uh, they wouldn't let him in backstage, you know, that Louis had, uh, the, the, you know, how the situation backstage can be. So, this chap had a, um, photograph of George Lewis with him. He took a scrap of paper and he wrote, friend of, on it, clipped it to the picture of George Lewis, and sent it in, and Louis didn't say bring him in. Louis came out to meet him, and brought him in himself. Um, and, um. I once heard a rumor, and I think this was just a rumor, that, that, that, that Louis had, at one point, considered, or even said something about having George Lewis playing his band. If he did, I never knew anything about it. No, I don't. No, I don't, I don't think that's true. Uh, unless Louis may have mentioned it to somebody, um, I know he never mentioned it to George. Uh, I would, I would say that was one of the multitudinous rumors that spring up in the jazz world. Yes. Because I knew nothing about it. Yes. Because I knew nothing about it. What do you think the, uh, impression that George Lewis band made on the kind of younger college audiences that he was playing for in that time? They loved it. Oh, they loved it. They loved it. Oh. Oh. Where were some of the college places you played? Okay. There, there was Ohio State, Purdue, Brown, that'd be in the East, um, college in Vermont. Oh dear.
Very well done. Amherst?

No, not Amherst. Not Williams. Amherst isn't in Vermont, it's in my own state. Um, not Bennington, that's a women's college. I can't remember them all, but there were a great many. There were a great many of them. Then there was a St. Paul's, a preparatory school, prep school in Massachusetts very late. Uh, uh, uh, uh. Like that? Yes, Alvin Kershaw arranged the date. Oh, that's funny, he's never on that. And, uh, no, he's moved somewhere else. I don't know where. I'll have to ask George. Isn't he in Peterborough? Not anymore. He was. Oh yes, and of course the band played in Peterborough. They played at a very informal type thing in Peterborough for, uh, for Al Kershaw. Uh, and in the middle of winter, ooh. Describe for me if you can. The very first time you had, when you said you went down to Los Angeles, had them in bed. I can't. I can't. I can't. It was such an overwhelming thing. It really was. It's not a thing I can put in words. Uh, I went in, I got there, they told me, when I cried, I called them on the phone and I said, must I make reservations? They said, yes, but don't expect us to hold them past a half hour before we open. Get here early? Well, I got there way early. And, uh, I remember I asked one of the cocktail waitresses if it would be possible for me to meet George Lewis. And she said, oh, of course. And she called him, uh, over and, uh, we sat at the bar and had a drink. And, of course, I was, I couldn't believe it was true. And, uh, Lawrence was there, and drag, and the whole group. And, um, George showed me just where to sit so I'd get the best sound and so forth. And he, I mentioned a number of numbers, he played them all for me. And, uh, it, it was overwhelming. It really was. I think, I think it's almost impossible for anyone to describe how they felt the first time they heard that real George Lewis group, with Lawrence and the whole group. It's, it's something you can't put in words. I went back to the hotel, as I say, and the world was all golden sound, you know? Oh. And, uh, I could hear it in my ears all night. Yeah. And, uh, it, it, it, to me, it was a, it's a very overwhelming experience, if you dig that music and really love it. Yes, I know. Let me think, there was one thing, this is something you may or may not know about this, and I just can't remember the man's name. Um, uh, what's his name, that record company? Good Time Jazz. Oh! Now, you remember, there's a very nice man, he's sort of fat. Yeah, uh, sure, Dave Stewart. Not Dave Stewart. Not Dave Stewart. Oh. No, no. Um, what is his name? Keith again. Yeah. A very nice man, kind of. Yeah, he's fat, uh, distinctly fat. But he, uh, not, not Mr. Koenig, there's another man, there's another man in that. Oh, Mr. Koenig. But he, he, he was, he was down here a year ago, and then, he told me that, that Good Time Jazz had recorded the George Lewis band playing in the Beverly Cabins for a year. Beverly Cabins for a regular concert, around about that time, 54. And that they were going to- No, I think it was before that. Maybe. It was before that. They recorded him there, and I believe they, uh, But the records never sold like a day, anyway. Whether they recorded him in, uh, at the Hangover Club in, uh, San Francisco or not, I don't know. I know Lester came up there and George refused to sign a contract with him. Uh, an exclusive contract. And, uh, but, very fat. I just can't- Isn't that funny? I always have trouble remembering that man. I can't think who you mean. He came- You know, there is a picture in my mind of a short, very fat man, but he doesn't tie up with anything in particular. He now sort of has his own record company, some kind of thing. And, uh, he was responsible for the issue of some of the early George Rose records, where he did Willie the Weeper and, uh, the- Yes, that was a good time, yes. But I just- Doesn't matter anyway. It's not important. No. It's- It's- It's- It's- Um. Um. Um. Um. Well, one thing I did want to ask you about was about the character of David in the Five Moved Stones. Well, the character of David is no one in—that is not based on any individual. But the character of Grant is more or less based on George Lewis. The character of who? Grant. The grandfather. Oh, I see. The grandfather. Yes. Not, of course, completely. I mean, George is a well-known clarinetist, and Grant in Five Moved Stones was just a man who played banjo locally, and there were some differences. But as far as his character and his personality, I admit it was frankly pretty much George Lewis. So much so that Molly Moon came down here not long ago. Her husband is the national director of publicity for the NAACP. And she went to Preservation Hall in the hope of hearing George. She didn't know him and hadn't heard him. And she walked in the hall and she said, there's Gramp! And—but that character is. But the character of David, who is the protagonist in the book, is not anyone in particular. The young man, sort of a composite of, you know—let me just ask you one other thing I had in mind. George did have an exclusive contract at one time, but— That's right. Do you know anything about that? I—I—oh, yes, I set it up. I had been wanting George to settle down to one company for a long time. And I went and I talked with Norman Grant. Ooh! But we finally set up a fairly, uh, a fairly nice arrangement. It was for two years. And it called for two or three records a year. I've—I've forgotten. I mean albums. And, uh, at the time of its expiration, Norman, uh, had, uh, was sold to that other company. And then George's health was very bad at that time. Which is when he was having those bad angina attacks. It didn't seem safe to—or fair, really, to the company. Although, heaven knows when the day that record companies, um, with one exception, which is Alfred Lyon, God love it. Uh, the day that record companies are completely fair to artists is the day that I'm really— Okay, we're just—I'll just say this is, uh, January the 5th, 1969. And I'm interviewing Bob Green. Right.
In New Orleans.
In New Orleans. All right, Bob. Now, uh, when was the first time you—you had, uh, Joel Schultz's band play? Do you remember?

Yes, I think it was January 62. I had been in Washington and just decided to go with the government. Had a few days, came down here, uh, and was wandering on the street and past Preservation Hall, which I had not even heard of up until that date. And, uh, was with a friend, and I said, my God, that sounds like George Lewis. And I sort of blindly pushed in past Sandy, past the basket, didn't stop, opened the door, and I said, my God, it is George Lewis. And, uh, I hadn't heard him play since, I think it was 1946 when he was in New York at the Starbizzen Casino with Funk, which in itself was a startling experience, walking in and suddenly hearing this sound. And all you knew prior to that time were the Condon records and Wild Bill Davidson and those big clothes.
Yes. Let's go back to the Starbizzen Casino because, uh, maybe you can describe the whole—the whole set up there and the impression when you walked in the door and what was going on.

It was overwhelming. It was a room such as I'd never seen, this huge ballroom with the walls sort of a cream color, tables all around, a dance floor cleared in the middle, with a great crystal chandelier hanging down with—that had these little, uh, surfaces on it. And as it revolved, lights played off it and reflected, rainbow-colored almost, off the walls. And over in the far end, this great band with George and Bunk, Baby Dives, Jim Robinson, I guess Alton Purnell on piano that year, and Marrero. I don't know. And, uh, Slowdrag. This is in the fall of 45. This I don't remember. This was the first year Bunk was up there.
Because he made two trips to Danville back in the spring of 46.

I know. With Danille. With Danille. Danille was with him then, yes. And, uh, it was incredible. We had never—Nicks had been the only place that I'd ever heard live jazz before. I was early twenties. And suddenly walking into this room and hearing this power coming off the bandstand, with Bunk and George cutting through and filling in and Jim bringing up the bottom. And, uh, later during that—during the season they were there, I got a chance to speak to Bunk. And I remember—he's very nice. He was standing over in the corner. It was a quiet moment during an intermission. He said, uh, boy, I've had these—this iron against my teeth for too long now. These are all borrowed notes. And one felt that he knew exactly who he was and what he was doing, and how he had been brought back, and how little time actually there was for him.
Mm.
I didn't speak—as I remember—get a chance to speak to George during that time.
Had you heard music like that before?

Never. Never. Uh, I started with, uh, really the Benny Goodman Camel Caravan on Wednesday nights, and then bought some Benny Goodman records. Uh, had a few Beidebeck records. Uh, eventually got the Commodore records, and had never heard what a New Orleans band sounded like, and didn't know the difference between two beat and four beat. People talked of New Orleans style and Chicago style, and I didn't know there was a difference. They never heard it.
Mm. What was different about this music when he first had it? What was the impression you got about it that this was something different?

He felt you were on a locomotive, and just holding on for all you were worth, and it was just chugging, and you were—and the wind was just coming back. It—it—it—instead of one ensemble and everyone taking solos and taking turns, this whole band, this great machine, that worked and seemed to envelop everyone, the hundreds of people who were in the casino. It was quite extraordinary.
Did you go there several times?
Went there quite often. Went with Bill Grauer. Quite often we were classmates at Columbia. And then went the, uh, following year when Don Ullo was there. Mm.
So you did get a good impression of it?

Got a good impression of it. And got a, uh, it was the quality of the sound which was unforgettable, and I've heard a lot of New Orleans music since, played some of it, but the quality of that initial exposure, I will never forget. It's almost like when you're a kid and you look up and see the stars for the first time.
Well, then, uh, you—then you didn't hear George again until 62.
I heard George on records, and I wrote some liner notes for a Blue Note album that George did, but I didn't hear him in person until 62.
Then, who was he playing with? Can you remember who he was playing with in Preservation Hall?
Uh, Jim was there. That's all I remember. That's all I remember.

You know, I mean, that, that so-called All-Star band, the guitar and the slow track, they had quite a good band playing there on weekends, I think. They used to have that band on Saturday in the United States.
No. Perhaps it was. I don't know. I know Jim was there.
Did the—how did the music sound then in 62, as compared to your earlier members?

Um, George sounded the same, Jim sounded the same, but I didn't get the feeling of the tremendous size and the tremendous power that that Bunk band had. And I think part of it was due to the size of Preservation Hall. There just isn't enough room to really project. Uh, but the quality, it had exactly the same sound. Yeah. And again, it was this startling thing, like you'd suddenly been thrown in the lake, you know, what's happened? Here it is again. This instant recognition that this is special and fine. And, uh, immediately it knocked out all other jazz for me, except for the Morton recordings.
Okay, so then, now tell us about the—you went to Japan. You were into France. You were in Japan at the same time the store was there, weren't you?

I was in Japan visiting a cousin who lives in Tokyo in 63. This was the summer, I think August 63. And, uh, was wandering around Shibuya, which is the area in which he lived. And each—this is a small section of Tokyo, and it has its own small bar district and red light district, whatever. And it's up a hill behind some buildings and it's alleyways. And I was walking alone, feeling very western and very out of place. When suddenly this same sound that I'd heard in 1945 comes banging out onto the street. And it's a record of bunk and George Lewis. And it froze me in my tracks, was the last thing I expected to hear. And, again, blindly, I—there was a doorway and I just went in. And there was this smoke-filled room, oh, twenty feet by twenty, if that. Tables. Many Japanese sitting at it, drinking coffee. It was the swing coffee house in Shibuya. Later I found there were two coffee houses in the chain. This was one of them. And the little waitress came up to me. Her name, it turned out later, was Sayuri Yamamoto. And on the walls—I stood there and she asked me what I wanted and I couldn't talk. On the walls were pictures of George Lewis, bunk. In the back, over on the left, was a turntable, which—with, uh, against the wall a couple of huge speakers and a rack of records. And all of these records were George Lewis and Bunk Johnson. But there were more George Lewis records there than anything else. I couldn't believe it. And this is—this was their stock and trade. Japanese would come—come to the swing coffee house in Shibuya to listen to records and drink this tall iced coffee over—overly sweetened. They sat there. So, uh, they had some pictures of George on the wall and they had a excerpt centerfold from Time—Life magazine had done a story on New Orleans jazz and there it was not even framed. And, uh, you just pasted it on the wall. So, the little waitress, Sayuri Yamamoto, noticed how interested I was and, uh, said, George Lewis, I—I said, I—I—I know him. I've—I've heard him play. And, uh, she told me, and, uh, she told me, and very hesitant in English, he was coming to Japan, which was the first knowledge I had. I said, if he comes to Japan, if he comes to Tokyo, I'm sure I will see him. And our eyes lit up—someone who might know George Lewis. I said, somehow I will bring you his autograph and you can put it up on the wall next to the pictures. I left. Called the American Embassy. They didn't know when Lewis was coming to Japan. Finally, I forget how, I found the hotel that they were going to stay at. The name escapes me. And called the hotel and they had arrived the previous day or were to arrive the following day, whatever—this was several days after the initial encounter at the Swing. And I went over there and there was Jaffe and Sandy and George Lewis, uh, Manny Sales, Joe Watkins, Papa John Joseph, Joe Robichaux, Punch Miller, whoever left out, and, uh, Louis Nelson. And this was the band that was to tour Japan. It was—they had arrived—when I arrived at the hotel, they had arrived in Japan the previous day. And they had obviously been very tired. This was the following evening, late afternoon. And here they were in a foreign country, not knowing where to go, feeling a little bit lonely, a little bit out of place. Saw George, we greeted one another. I had played with George during that first visit to Preservation Hall. New Orleans was still segregated at that time. And somehow the band had stopped playing. George was putting away his clarinet. I got to the piano and I remember playing Whining Boy. And George put together his clarinet. And Jaffe's closed the shutters and we played together, which was a very moving experience, because it was really just the second time I'd seen him since the bunk days. That was the first time you've played with him. That was the first time I played with him. So that when I did greet him in the hotel in Japan, he knew who I was. I certainly knew who he was. And it was a nice hello. They were thinking, where should they go that evening? And I said, well, I don't know whether you'd be interested. I knew quite well they probably would be. I said, but there's a little coffee house, which I think I can find, which I think would entertain you. I have nothing but your records there, George, and your pictures on the wall. And they worship you there. So everyone's eyes lit up. Let's go. We piled into two taxi cabs. And about nine o'clock, I forget what day of the week this was, I don't think it was a weekend, probably a Thursday night, something like that. We arrived at the Swing coffee house.
S.W. Island.

Right. And Jaffe said, you go first. And behind me stood Lewis and George Lewis and Nelson and the rest of the band. So I knocked on the door of the Swing. The door opened and little Sayori Yamamoto appears. And she looked at me and again, in very hesitant English, said, do you have the autograph? I said, no, but I have George Lewis. And the door opened and George Lewis came in. The place suddenly you could hear just a collective gasp. Everything stopped. And the musicians ended. And within ten seconds there wasn't standing room in that place. It filled with young Japanese who had never seen anything like it. And the band sat down at a couple of tables against the wall. Places were made for them. And it was almost a religious education. The man that this shrine had been built for had suddenly walked into it. And the adoration was, you could really feel it, which may have embarrassed George possibly. It was so obvious. They sat down and then began one of the loveliest jazz concerts I've ever heard. Because these men, without their instruments, sat there. And now over the vitrola, over the phonograph, came the sounds of George Lewis and Jim Robinson and whoever, but always George. And after each solo, the Japanese, in the swing, clapped. And the musician who took the solo, who was George Lewis, he stood up and took a bow. And this went on for about an hour and a half. The following morning, I must say, I walked through that little part of Tokyo and I think I could have run for mayor. Every Japanese, Konichiwa, Ohio, Gazzaro, nodded. And I said hello. I never realized I had so many friends. Then eventually, the following night, in order that the other swing coffee shop did not lose face, we went over there and paid a repeat visit. Of course, it was not a surprise because obviously they had been on the phone immediately.
Did you hear the George Lewis band playing in Japan? All the time. I traveled with them.
All the time. I traveled with them.
How were they received?

Beautifully. The first concert was at the Great Music Hall in Tokyo, which seems to be about the size of the Radio City Music Hall in New York. Absolutely crowded. Plush seats. You can't out nightclub the Japanese. This wasn't a nightclub. Just a huge theater. Huge balcony. Every seat taken. It seems some union in Japan was sponsoring this tour for their members. People interested in music, I think, could pay a certain fee and be invited to a certain number of concerts a year. This was one of the concerts on the list. And here was this audience, many of them I don't think knowing what to expect, although we later found out that many of the men who, Japanese, who appeared in the swing coffee shop that first night turned out to be Japanese musicians that we've become very friendly with since, who were in the neighborhood, gotten on the phone. And the band was just beautifully received. There was a big sign over the stage, George Lewis. I forget the first, but they played Alexander's Ragtime Band. And the last tune was Till We Meet Again with George, thanking them all for being there. And the young Japanese girls coming up with flowers and giving it to them. And the band just beautifully received.
Did you hear them in the Osaka? What was it?

Then, then there were several concerts in Tokyo. Then went to Osaka, to the Shin-Ozaka Hotel, where the band stayed and I stayed too. And there was a music hall around the corner. Again, absolutely huge, very plush. And now a fantastically enthusiastic response because Osaka was the center of the Japanese, the Dixieland Rascals, the Japanese band. And it was a fantastic And it was just mobbed. And terribly successful. And in the lobby of the hotel, there was a great chance for the Japanese to get to know the American musicians. Papa John, Joseph at 89, sitting there, either talking to a young, a Japanese infant or an elderly Japanese man. Neither speaking the other's language, but understanding each other perfectly for hours on end.

I believe they played in a soccer, but I think Jaffee said they played for something like 40 nights in a row. Yep. Is that right? He said that they were actually, that the festival hall where it was there, and they were actually packed out more every night.
Every night, 40 nights, I think roughly is correct. That is really extraordinary. Absolutely packed.
It's hard to imagine that happening in any city in the world. Yeah. So, what did George think of Japan? Did you ever hear him talking about it?

He loved it. He loved it. He loved the people of, I think the words that he, one of the records, George Lewis in Japan, his closing salutation to them or saying goodbye to them, I think it's completely honest, the lovely people of Japan. He was so pleased. He recognized fully their appreciation of what he was doing. Yes. And he responded to it. And all the musicians do. And Joe Watkins to this day still talks of Japan. He and Manny Sales and I bummed around together sometimes if we had an off evening and explored the little bars and pubs and they just loved it. Just loved it.

I think it's a great question. Let's, let's, let's, we can perhaps change the subject a little. Um, George's funeral was on Friday and you were not only there but playing in one of the bands. And perhaps you can, I mean this is, we're fairly close to this right now but you know in years of time people will want to know about the funeral I think. Perhaps you can say something about it and, uh, as you brought back in. The general, just describe what happened.

Well, like all New Orleans funerals, playing, I'm playing my bad borrowed cornet. It's not, it wasn't a bad cornet, I play it badly. Uh, meeting on the street corner. There's somewhat of a feeling that it's frivolous, I think. Uh, I'm not, in my tradition I'm not used to funerals being that much of a party. What impressed me so much, starting off at the hall with the Japanese and the Swedes and Frank DeMond and Charlie DeVore who'd come in from Minneapolis, starting this band was, how wonderful this is. What we are concerned is not a funeral but are our instruments okay? The drummer didn't have a strap for his drum, he had to fashion it out of a rope. Concerned with, was the head of the drum tight? Whose cornet? Were there enough, was there, did the mouthpiece fit? We were concerned with the trade of the man who was being buried and in that sense it was a continuation. And therefore, at that moment I realized my whole concept of funeral has to change. That this was acting out something. It was almost, I felt a ritualistic dance. This getting ready, it was George Lewis's last gig. This is what it felt like. And we were gonna play at George's last gig. And it was much more like a jazz job than a funeral. Although there was no pay involved.
Yes. Did you, um, were you in the church?

I was in the church, uh, of course as you know there was a gentle rain, it was misty, and, and a very Japanese weather as a matter of fact. Everything was very soft, very gray. Uh, went into the church, surprisingly found a seat, and stayed for the funeral. And then outside into the rain again.
What did you, what, uh, can you describe the service?

Uh, again I got the feeling of a ritualistic dance or chant rather than a service. I listened to the minister, uh, he started reading text, it didn't really make much sense, it didn't have much continuity, just as pure English. It didn't have much to do with George Lewis. And then his reading gradually began to take on rhythmic overtones, and it became a chant. And you felt that if it were only kept up a little longer, the whole audience would let go. It was, it was a catharsis. It was an emotional experience. What about the singing? The singing I wasn't overly impressed by. Wasn't overly impressed by. There were six other preachers there, and the dean of Winchester Cathedral would come to the church. And then from the center, sure. But I did think of, in the church of Papa John, once in Japan, I said to Papa John Joseph, who at 89 ought to know, I said, Papa John, you ought to know, where did jazz come from?
He said, from the Baptist church. Yes.
Well, I'm not saying I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that. I know that.

I know that. Well, I must say, I was, there was one song where a hymn was the same label that the choir leader sang himself. You know, there was a certain beat for the music. You know, there was an old color lady playing it sitting there and she had an umbrella and she was tapping it in time with the music. It just had a certain quality of atmosphere.
It was jazz. It was jazz.
Yeah.

Yeah. Then back out into the, into the rain and playing, close a walk. Then, uh, as the hearse passed again and then, uh, into Frank DeMond's old pickup truck, out to the cemetery, through the mud and sloshing through it. Really couldn't get near the grave. And, uh, disorganized somewhat, umbrellas, the band scattered all around. And yet, uh, the feeling of a strange mixture of a jazz job. Am I gonna play this old trumpet all right? Um, where are the other guys in the band? Poor George, I can't believe he's dead. I'm sorry it's raining. I'll never get the mud off my shoes. How could this have happened to George Lewis? All of these things going on at the same time. Um, I had a little flask with some vodka in it, at which point I downed the whole four ounces.
Um, what was your feeling about, was your feeling, how, how many times did you actually play with George Lewis or play with the fans? Many, many times.

I don't, we played a great deal in Japan together with the Japanese. I played at Preservation Hall with him, maybe 20 times. Um, very exciting to play with. And he did something that makes a, uh, a younger musician, not of the same caliber, feel very good. When you played, he listened. And if you made something pretty, he turned around and acknowledged it. Yes, and I think he always was very receptive. He heard. He knew what you were trying to do.

Which I think is something that in some way sets him apart from a lot of the other New Orleans musicians. I mean, I think in that sense George was especially receptive about music. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, what, do you find any difference playing with a, uh, say New Orleans Colored Band or a New Orleans Band as opposed to playing with the, the kind of people that you say in Washington? I mean, is there a difference in the music?

Well, so much so that I try not to play in Washington except solo because, uh, there, I find further north you go, the white musicians, this is not true in Europe. But in this country, uh, there's no concept of, of a band. There's no concept of ensemble. There are no concepts of different parts for the, for the instruments, the voicing. It's a concept of one ensemble and every man takes a solo and the drummer's always building a house and you have to try to overblow him. And, uh, in New Orleans the opposite is true. Yeah. So that there really is no, no comparison at all. And you'll find it with a New Orleans musician occasionally in the piano you'll fall into a riff and suddenly you'll hear the riff taken up. And, uh, rather than a solo, one instrument comes out in front but the others are pulsing behind it. So that it's so much easier playing piano because your wind instruments actually are assuming rhythmic functions with their riffs and they're coming in on their syncopation. So that it's so much easier to play with them. And with that lovely square four beat that just sets the tune going and then it seems to go by itself.

Um, how do you feel about George in relation to New Orleans jazz, uh, history let's say, and his position? And, um, how do you think people, uh, do you think you'll continue to be acknowledged or do you think you'll be considered greater when you get, when, as time goes on? Or do you think you'll be considered as long or, uh, do you have any sense of, uh, his position?

Yeah, I, I think, uh, you have to divide New Orleans jazz history into two periods. I think the original history and its death, its demise almost completely with your giant, with your Johnny Dodds and Ole Miss Simeon. And then, uh, nothing. And then the revival with George and Bonk. And then George Lewis emerging as really the, the great giant on the clarinet and maintaining this position. And the fact that this music ever got off the old scratchy 78s, I think, is in a large measure George's contribution. And the fact, no matter where in the world you go, kids playing clarinet are playing like him. They're not playing like Johnny Dodds. They're not playing like Ole Miss Simeon. They're playing like George Lewis. So in, in a sense, while I don't think you list him among the jazz greats of the early period, in many ways he proved to be greater and more durable than any of them. Mm-hmm. And his influence, I think, is stronger than Johnny Dodds, stronger than Jelly Roll Morton, uh, far stronger than a white musician, say, Beiderbeck. Uh, George Lewis lived and he happened now and he happened in our time and he ranked with the Giants. And now, when you go back and listen to the old records, you can fit George in and see what George, imagine what George would have done in, in these records and you realize how truly great he was.

Um, how do you feel about the future of this music in general? I mean, as we know in New Orleans, the younger, younger people in New Orleans really aren't thinking out of music. Um, how do you feel about the future in general? Not necessarily for the rest of it.

Mixed, mixed feelings, Tom. Uh, I think it's such a specialized art form it can get away from you unless you hear it and play it as often as possible. I think the tendency, there is, in any band, there's a tendency for a band to disintegrate, less ensemble and more solo. Uh, all over the world, really largely through George, uh, and the recordings, uh, young bands are playing New Orleans style. How deeply rooted this is, I don't know. You see, it isn't this present generation. It isn't the men between 40 and 50 who are playing now. It's, who's gonna come afterward. You see a boy like young Tom Sancton, who played at George's Wake, playing this incredibly beautiful George Lewis style clarinet. It gives you great hope. But I wonder who young Tom Sancton will be playing with in another 20 years.
And we might say here that, uh, Tom Sancton is from New Orleans, which is quite unusual.
That's right. New George, you heard him. Uh, what happens in another 20 years? I don't know.

Of course, we have bands like the Hall Brothers Band in Minneapolis, which are a young band, and they're playing, uh, I think very well in New Orleans style. Beautiful. Beautiful. Of course, there are really very few, it's almost the only band in the country that was in that class.
In England, you have Sammy Remington, superb musician. Beautiful George Lewis clarinet. Beautiful sax.

Well, actually I feel that it's hard to believe that music of the quality of New Orleans as I discussed, which I think is a very high quality, can really die out. I mean, I think there must always be people with sufficient musical, um, sensitivity to realize this is something quite exceptionally good. And one feels, perhaps optimistically, that it's got to survive somehow. I don't know.

I think now the chance is better than it was after the first, quote, death of New Orleans jazz, because it's on LP records and it's beautifully recorded and it's available, which was not true in 1945, when George and Bunk came back. So that this music has been so documented that it is possible now to imitate from the music and to grasp it from the music rather than just hearing it in person. So I, there, there's a legacy now that's been recorded and I think it's important.

If George, in a sense, does have pupils, and I had never actually studied personally under him, there are people who have, who have studied memory on his records, which, uh, I think means that he should, by all odds, continue to have quite a considerable influence.
But whether he will have the, the, the drummers and the piano men, uh, and the trombones and the, and the horns to back him, I don't know. I hope so. And I think so.
Right. Well, uh, is there anything else? I mean, just about running out here. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right.
Right. Right. Right.
Right. Right.

Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. And George, for no reason at all, bought me breakfast. We sat and had a long breakfast, maybe well over an hour. George Lewis had nothing he gained from me. He couldn't learn from me musically. There was no financial reward. He knew I cared. And I was leaving. It would be nice for him to buy me breakfast, which he did.

Yes, I should just say on this tape that when I saw George in hospital just before he died, about a week before he died, I told him I was going to Washington, which I... When I left, I knew I probably wouldn't see him again. He did say, you'll see Bob Green. You'll see Bob Green when he was in Washington. He said it two or three times. He did come down, of course, before he died.
I wasn't able to. I called. There were no more visitors, but I asked that my name be left. And evidently it was. So? Well, we're all poorer. Yeah.
Yeah. Well. Okay. Well, thanks so much, Bob. Good job. That's fine. One footnote.
I visited George in October out in Darmus Street in Algiers.
October of 16th?

Yeah. And he was ill. And he said, Bob, when I go, I hope I go like Papa John. I hope I go on the bandstand. He said, I never want to quit playing. I want to go like Papa John. Mm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
